claim: A first pregnancy before age 22 lowers breast cancer risk.
source: While a first pregnancy before age 22 lowers breast cancer risk, a pregnancy after age 35 significantly increases life-long breast cancer risk.
evidence: This is supported by citation to epidemiological literature (MacMahon et al., 1970; Polyak, 2006; Schedin, 2006) as stated in the Introduction.

claim: A pregnancy after age 35 significantly increases life-long breast cancer risk.
source: While a first pregnancy before age 22 lowers breast cancer risk, a pregnancy after age 35 significantly increases life-long breast cancer risk.
evidence: This is supported by citation to epidemiological literature (MacMahon et al., 1970; Polyak, 2006; Schedin, 2006) as stated in the Introduction.

claim: Pregnancy causes apoptosis evasion in preexisting early lesions in the breast.
source: We show in mice that pregnancy has different effects on the few early lesions that have already developed in the otherwise normal breast—it causes apoptosis evasion and accelerated progression to cancer.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F-H demonstrating reduced apoptosis in early lesions of parous mice compared to virgin mice.

claim: Pregnancy causes accelerated progression to cancer in preexisting early lesions.
source: We show in mice that pregnancy has different effects on the few early lesions that have already developed in the otherwise normal breast—it causes apoptosis evasion and accelerated progression to cancer.
evidence: This is supported by tumor-free survival data in Figures 1A and 2A showing faster tumor development in parous mice.

claim: The apoptosis evasion in preexisting early lesions is due to STAT5 signaling going astray.
source: The apoptosis evasion is due to the normally tightly controlled STAT5 signaling going astray—these precancerous cells activate STAT5 in response to pregnancy/lactation hormones and maintain STAT5 activation even during involution, thus preventing the apoptosis normally initiated by oncoprotein and involution.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3A-B showing elevated pSTAT5 in early lesions of parous mice at involution.

claim: Precancerous cells activate STAT5 in response to pregnancy/lactation hormones.
source: The apoptosis evasion is due to the normally tightly controlled STAT5 signaling going astray—these precancerous cells activate STAT5 in response to pregnancy/lactation hormones and maintain STAT5 activation even during involution, thus preventing the apoptosis normally initiated by oncoprotein and involution.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3A showing increased pSTAT5 in early lesions during pregnancy and lactation.

claim: Precancerous cells maintain STAT5 activation even during involution.
source: The apoptosis evasion is due to the normally tightly controlled STAT5 signaling going astray—these precancerous cells activate STAT5 in response to pregnancy/lactation hormones and maintain STAT5 activation even during involution, thus preventing the apoptosis normally initiated by oncoprotein and involution.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3A-B showing persistent pSTAT5 in early lesions at involution day 10 (I10).

claim: Short-term anti-STAT5 treatment of lactation-completed mice bearing early lesions eliminates the increased risk after a pregnancy.
source: Short-term anti-STAT5 treatment of lactation-completed mice bearing early lesions eliminates the increased risk after a pregnancy.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6I-J showing that C188-9 treatment improved tumor-free survival and reduced tumor incidence in parous mice.

claim: Parous mice infected with RCAS-caErbb2 developed tumors significantly faster than virgin control mice.
source: While caErbB2 induced tumors much more rapidly than Wnt1, each parous group developed tumors significantly faster than its corresponding virgin control cohort (Figure 1A; Figure 2A) and with higher tumor multiplicity (Figure 1B; Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is directly shown in the Kaplan-Meier survival curves in Figure 1A with p=0.004.

claim: Parous mice infected with RCAS-caErbb2 had higher tumor multiplicity than virgin control mice.
source: While caErbB2 induced tumors much more rapidly than Wnt1, each parous group developed tumors significantly faster than its corresponding virgin control cohort (Figure 1A; Figure 2A) and with higher tumor multiplicity (Figure 1B; Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B with p=0.038.

claim: Parous mice infected with RCAS-Wnt1 developed tumors significantly faster than virgin control mice.
source: While caErbB2 induced tumors much more rapidly than Wnt1, each parous group developed tumors significantly faster than its corresponding virgin control cohort (Figure 1A; Figure 2A) and with higher tumor multiplicity (Figure 1B; Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is shown in the Kaplan-Meier survival curves in Figure 2A with p=0.03.

claim: The great majority of tumors initiated by Erbb2 appeared at least 7 weeks after the completion of pregnancy.
source: The great majority of tumors initiated by Erbb2 appeared at least 7 weeks after the completion of pregnancy, beyond the equivalent window of time considered to be PABC in women (Borges and Schedin, 2012), and all tumors initiated by Wnt1 appeared more than 36 weeks after the completion of pregnancy.
evidence: This is based on observation of tumor latency data and comparison to the definition of pregnancy-associated breast cancer (PABC) from the cited literature.

claim: All tumors initiated by Wnt1 appeared more than 36 weeks after the completion of pregnancy.
source: The great majority of tumors initiated by Erbb2 appeared at least 7 weeks after the completion of pregnancy, beyond the equivalent window of time considered to be PABC in women (Borges and Schedin, 2012), and all tumors initiated by Wnt1 appeared more than 36 weeks after the completion of pregnancy.
evidence: This is based on observation of tumor latency data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Pregnancy stimulates the long-term cancer risk from mammary cells that have already acquired an oncogenic mutation.
source: Therefore, we conclude that pregnancy stimulates the long-term cancer risk from mammary cells that have already acquired an oncogenic mutation.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the tumor latency and characteristics data presented in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: At 1.5 weeks post injection, the number of total early lesions was similar between virgin and P7.5 mice.
source: At 1.5 weeks post injection, the number of total early lesions (defined as any hyperplastic ductal foci comprised of more than three layers of epithelial cells that stained positive for the provirus-encoded oncogene product) was similar between the virgin and P7.5 mice (Figure 1D), consistent with their similar rates of initial infection.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D with p=0.8.

claim: By 5.5 and 8.5 weeks post-viral injection, the total number of early lesions was greater in L12 and I10 groups than in the respective age-matched virgin mice.
source: By 5.5 and 8.5 weeks post-viral injection, however, the total number of early lesions was greater in L12 and I10 groups than in the respective age-matched virgin mice (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D with p=0.02 for both time points.

claim: By 8.5 weeks post infection, the average lesion area was significantly larger in I10 mice than in the age-matched virgin animals.
source: By 8.5 weeks post infection, the average lesion area was also significantly larger in I10 mice than in the age-matched virgin animals (Figure 1C,E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1E with p=0.04.

claim: Pregnancy accelerates carcinogenesis by promoting the advancement of early lesions from cells that have already activated oncogenic signaling.
source: Therefore, we conclude that pregnancy accelerates carcinogenesis by promoting the advancement of early lesions from cells that have already activated oncogenic signaling.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the data showing increased lesion number and size in parous mice (Figure 1D-E).

claim: Early lesions in P7.5 and virgin control mice had similar proliferative indices based on staining for Ki67.
source: Early lesions in P7.5 and virgin control mice had similar proliferative indices based on staining for Ki67 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) and pHistone3 (data not shown), suggesting that the already high proliferation in oncogene-activated cells cannot be further elevated by pregnancy.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 with p=0.4.

claim: Proliferation remained comparable between the early lesions of L12 mice and those of age-matched virgin mice.
source: Proliferation remained comparable between the early lesions of L12 mice and those of age-matched virgin mice.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 with p=0.9.

claim: Proliferation was lower in the early lesions of I10 mice than in those of age-matched virgin mice.
source: It was even lower in the early lesions of I10 mice than in those of age-matched virgin mice, suggesting that the molecular network activated in normal epithelia at involution to arrest the cell cycle (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B) also operates in these premalignant cells.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 with p<0.01.

claim: Pregnancy-induced acceleration of carcinogenesis from mutated cells does not result from increased proliferation.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that pregnancy-induced acceleration of carcinogenesis from mutated cells does not result from increased proliferation.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the proliferation data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 showing no increase or even decrease in proliferation in parous early lesions.

claim: Apoptosis was activated in the early lesions of virgin mice at all three time points (1.5, 5.5, and 8.5 weeks post infection) compared to normal ducts.
source: As expected, apoptosis was activated in the early lesions of virgin mice at all three time points (1.5, 5.5, and 8.5 weeks post infection) compared to normal ducts (Figure 1G,H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1G-H with p values of 0.01, 0.02, and 0.001 for the three time points.

claim: The level of apoptosis was significantly lower in early lesions of the parous group at all three time points than those in early lesions of the respective virgin mice.
source: However, the level of apoptosis was significantly lower in early lesions of the parous group at all three time points than those in early lesions of the respective virgin mice (Figure 1G); it became either comparable to the baseline level in normal ducts during pregnancy and lactation or even significantly lower than that during involution (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1G with p values of 0.01, 0.02, and 0.001 for the three time points.

claim: With a pregnancy preexisting premalignant mammary cells overcome both the apoptotic response to an oncoprotein and the robust cell death at involution.
source: These observations demonstrate that with a pregnancy preexisting premalignant mammary cells overcome both the apoptotic response to an oncoprotein and the robust cell death at involution, which normally clears the large mass of cells gained during pregnancy/lactation.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the apoptosis data in Figure 1G-H showing reduced apoptosis in parous early lesions.

claim: The early lesions of I10 mice harbored abundant numbers of cells positive for p53, Bax, and Bak.
source: However, despite their very low apoptotic rate, the early lesions of I10 mice harbored abundant numbers of cells positive for p53, Bax, and Bak (data not shown), suggesting that as in virgin mice oncogene-activated cells in parous glands are fully capable of activating p53 and its pro-apoptosis targets, but these precancerous cells nevertheless evade apoptosis.
evidence: This is based on immunostaining data (not shown in figures).

claim: Oncogene-activated cells in parous glands are fully capable of activating p53 and its pro-apoptosis targets, but these precancerous cells nevertheless evade apoptosis.
source: However, despite their very low apoptotic rate, the early lesions of I10 mice harbored abundant numbers of cells positive for p53, Bax, and Bak (data not shown), suggesting that as in virgin mice oncogene-activated cells in parous glands are fully capable of activating p53 and its pro-apoptosis targets, but these precancerous cells nevertheless evade apoptosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of p53, Bax, and Bak despite low apoptosis.

claim: The activated form of STAT5 is detected in the great majority of epithelial mammary cells, and at increased levels, during pregnancy and lactation.
source: While found in some mammary cells prior to pregnancy, the activated form of STAT5 is detected in the great majority of epithelial mammary cells, and at increased levels, during pregnancy and lactation (Liu et al., 1995; Wagner and Rui, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Liu et al., 1995; Wagner and Rui, 2008).

claim: Placental lactogen and prolactin (PRL) activate PRLR, leading to the recruitment of Jak2 and Jak2-mediated phosphorylation and activation of STAT5.
source: This is because placental lactogen and prolactin (PRL) activate PRLR, leading to the recruitment of Jak2 and Jak2-mediated phosphorylation and activation of STAT5 (Hennighausen and Robinson, 1998; Haricharan and Li, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Hennighausen and Robinson, 1998; Haricharan and Li, 2014).

claim: At the onset of involution, STAT5 is rapidly deactivated to allow programmed death of excess cells accumulated during pregnancy and lactation.
source: At the onset of involution, STAT5 is rapidly deactivated to allow programmed death of excess cells accumulated during pregnancy and lactation (Li et al., 1997; Hennighausen and Robinson, 2001; Kreuzaler et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Li et al., 1997; Hennighausen and Robinson, 2001; Kreuzaler et al., 2011).

claim: Transgenic expression of constitutively active Stat5 mutants in mammary glands leads to increased mammary cell survival, hyperplasia, and even occasional tumors.
source: Transgenic expression of constitutively active Stat5 mutants in mammary glands leads to increased mammary cell survival, hyperplasia, and even occasional tumors (Iavnilovitch et al., 2002; Dong et al., 2010; Vafaizadeh et al., 2012), while Stat5 heterozygosity delays mammary tumorigenesis in mice carrying a transgenic oncogene (Humphreys and Hennighausen, 1999; Ren et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Iavnilovitch et al., 2002; Dong et al., 2010; Vafaizadeh et al., 2012).

claim: Stat5 heterozygosity delays mammary tumorigenesis in mice carrying a transgenic oncogene.
source: Transgenic expression of constitutively active Stat5 mutants in mammary glands leads to increased mammary cell survival, hyperplasia, and even occasional tumors (Iavnilovitch et al., 2002; Dong et al., 2010; Vafaizadeh et al., 2012), while Stat5 heterozygosity delays mammary tumorigenesis in mice carrying a transgenic oncogene (Humphreys and Hennighausen, 1999; Ren et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Humphreys and Hennighausen, 1999; Ren et al., 2002).

claim: pSTAT5 is detected frequently in human breast early lesions (ductal carcinomas in situ) and to a lesser degree in invasive breast cancers.
source: pSTAT5 is also detected frequently in human breast early lesions (ductal carcinomas in situ) and to a lesser degree in invasive breast cancers (Cotarla et al., 2004; Nevalainen et al., 2004; Peck et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Cotarla et al., 2004; Nevalainen et al., 2004; Peck et al., 2011).

claim: The average percentage of pSTAT5+ cells per lesion was significantly higher in the parous mice at P7.5, L12, and I10 than in the corresponding age-matched virgin groups.
source: Therefore, we asked whether preexisting precancerous cells in our parous cohort might evade apoptosis by exploiting this normally well-regulated cell survival pathway. The average percentage of pSTAT5+ cells per lesion was significantly higher in the parous mice at P7.5, L12, and I10 than in the corresponding age-matched virgin groups, while cells positive for total STAT5 were readily detectable with comparable frequency in virgin vs parous lesions as expected (Kazansky et al., 1995) (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1 with p values of 0.04, 0.04, and p<0.01 for the three time points.

claim: >70% of the preneoplastic lesions in the parous cohort harbored >5% pSTAT5+ cells.
source: Furthermore, >70% of the preneoplastic lesions in the parous cohort harbored >5% pSTAT5+ cells (Figure 3B) and were thus defined as pSTAT5+ lesions (this cut-off was chosen because pSTAT5 positivity at this frequency correlated significantly with increased survival as shown below in Figure 3C), while <25% of the lesions in the virgin cohort were scored pSTAT5+.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B.

claim: <25% of the lesions in the virgin cohort were scored pSTAT5+.
source: Furthermore, >70% of the preneoplastic lesions in the parous cohort harbored >5% pSTAT5+ cells (Figure 3B) and were thus defined as pSTAT5+ lesions (this cut-off was chosen because pSTAT5 positivity at this frequency correlated significantly with increased survival as shown below in Figure 3C), while <25% of the lesions in the virgin cohort were scored pSTAT5+.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Premalignant mammary cells respond to pregnancy and lactation hormones by activating STAT5, as their normal counterparts do.
source: These data suggest that premalignant mammary cells respond to pregnancy and lactation hormones by activating STAT5, as their normal counterparts do (Figure 3A inset); however—unlike their normal counterparts—they continue to maintain high levels of pSTAT5 even during involution (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is inferred from the data in Figure 3A showing increased pSTAT5 during pregnancy and lactation.

claim: Premalignant mammary cells continue to maintain high levels of pSTAT5 even during involution, unlike their normal counterparts.
source: These data suggest that premalignant mammary cells respond to pregnancy and lactation hormones by activating STAT5, as their normal counterparts do (Figure 3A inset); however—unlike their normal counterparts—they continue to maintain high levels of pSTAT5 even during involution (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B with p=0.03.

claim: When early lesions in I10 mice were analyzed, increased levels of the STAT5 prosurvival transcriptional targets BclXL and Bcl2 as well as cyclinD1 were detected compared to early lesions in age-matched virgin mice.
source: Consistent with STAT5 activation, when early lesions in I10 mice were further analyzed, we detected increased levels of the STAT5 prosurvival transcriptional targets BclXL (Socolovsky et al., 2001) and Bcl2 (Lord et al., 2000; Hand et al., 2010) as well as cyclinD1 (Matsumura et al., 1999; Brockman et al., 2002) compared to early lesions in age-matched virgin mice (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2 with p values of p<0.01, p=0.002, p=0.01, and p=0.04.

claim: There was a strong inverse correlation between the percentage of pSTAT5+ cells and the level of apoptosis in parous early lesions.
source: Importantly, there was a strong inverse correlation between the percentage of pSTAT5+ cells and the level of apoptosis in these parous early lesions (Figure 3C), suggesting a causal relationship between pSTAT5 levels and cell survival.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C with p=0.005 and R²=0.6604.

claim: <1% of cells in virgin and parous early lesions were pSTAT1+ or pSTAT6+, and <2% were pSTAT3+.
source: Of note, <1% of cells in virgin and parous early lesions were pSTAT1+ or pSTAT6+, and <2% were pSTAT3+ (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), indicating that among the STATs known to be activated in the mammary gland (Chapman et al., 1999; Watson, 2001; Hennighausen and Robinson, 2005; Khaled et al., 2007), STAT5 is the predominant family member activated in parous early lesions.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: STAT5 is the predominant STAT family member activated in parous early lesions.
source: Of note, <1% of cells in virgin and parous early lesions were pSTAT1+ or pSTAT6+, and <2% were pSTAT3+ (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), indicating that among the STATs known to be activated in the mammary gland (Chapman et al., 1999; Watson, 2001; Hennighausen and Robinson, 2005; Khaled et al., 2007), STAT5 is the predominant family member activated in parous early lesions.
evidence: This is inferred from the low levels of other pSTATs compared to pSTAT5 shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Wnt1-initiated lesions in age-matched parous mice exhibited improved survival compared to lesions in virgin mice.
source: Compared to the lesions in virgin mice, the Wnt1-initiated lesions in age-matched parous mice exhibited improved survival (Figure 2D) and an increased percentage of pSTAT5+ cells (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), while also showing reduced proliferation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) similar to their RCAS-caErbb2-injected counterparts.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D with p=0.02.

claim: Wnt1-initiated lesions in age-matched parous mice had an increased percentage of pSTAT5+ cells compared to lesions in virgin mice.
source: Compared to the lesions in virgin mice, the Wnt1-initiated lesions in age-matched parous mice exhibited improved survival (Figure 2D) and an increased percentage of pSTAT5+ cells (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), while also showing reduced proliferation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) similar to their RCAS-caErbb2-injected counterparts.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E with p<0.001.

claim: Wnt1-initiated lesions in age-matched parous mice showed reduced proliferation compared to lesions in virgin mice.
source: Compared to the lesions in virgin mice, the Wnt1-initiated lesions in age-matched parous mice exhibited improved survival (Figure 2D) and an increased percentage of pSTAT5+ cells (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), while also showing reduced proliferation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) similar to their RCAS-caErbb2-injected counterparts.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A with p=0.03.

claim: pSTAT5 was readily detected in mammary epithelia of MMTV-Erbb2 transgenic mice at involution day 10, but not in mammary glands of age-matched non-transgenic virgin mice.
source: In addition, we asked whether parity leads to persistent STAT5 activation in classical transgenic models of breast cancer. pSTAT5 was readily detected in mammary epithelia of MMTV-Erbb2 transgenic mice at involution day 10, but not in mammary glands of age-matched non-transgenic virgin mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Parity-induced persistent activation of STAT5 in precancerous cells is not limited to a specific oncogenic mutation or a unique model of breast cancer.
source: Together, these data suggest that parity-induced persistent activation of STAT5 in precancerous cells is not limited to a specific oncogenic mutation or a unique model of breast cancer.
evidence: This conclusion is based on observations in multiple models (RCAS-caErbb2, RCAS-Wnt1, MMTV-Erbb2) showing similar pSTAT5 activation patterns.

claim: PRLR was readily detected in caErbb2-induced early lesions, with the percentage of positive cells being threefold higher than that in early lesions of age-matched virgin mice.
source: As shown in Figure 3F, while being diminished in normal epithelia by I10, PRLR was readily detected in caErbb2-induced early lesions, with the percentage of positive cells being threefold higher than that in early lesions of age-matched virgin mice (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3F with p=0.02.

claim: Oncogene-activated mammary cells, unlike their normal counterparts, fail to degrade PRLR at the onset of involution.
source: These data suggest that oncogene-activated mammary cells, unlike their normal counterparts, fail to degrade PRLR at the onset of involution.
evidence: This is inferred from the persistent PRLR expression in early lesions at I10 shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The inactivated form of GSK3β, pS9-GSK3β, was readily detected by immunohistochemistry in caErbb2-initiated early lesions in parous mice while it was not found in normal mammary cells.
source: Indeed, the inactivated form of GSK3β, pS9-GSK3β, was readily detected by immunohistochemistry in caErbb2-initiated early lesions in parous mice while it was not found in normal mammary cells (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E.

claim: In early lesions of virgin mice, an elevated and similar level of pS9-GSK3β was detected due to ErbB2-mediated oncogenic signaling.
source: In early lesions of virgin mice, an elevated and similar level of pS9-GSK3β was also detected due to ErbB2-mediated oncogenic signaling.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E.

claim: During pregnancy and lactation preexisting premalignant mammary cells activate the PRLR-Jak2-STAT5 signaling cascade as normal mammary cells do, but after the onset of involution, these oncogene-activated cells aberrantly maintain an activated state of this pathway likely via oncoprotein-mediated inactivation of GSK3β preventing timely PRLR degradation.
source: Together, these data suggest that during pregnancy and lactation preexisting premalignant mammary cells activate the PRLR-Jak2-STAT5 signaling cascade as normal mammary cells do, but after the onset of involution, these oncogene-activated cells aberrantly maintain an activated state of this pathway likely via oncoprotein-mediated inactivation of GSK3β preventing timely PRLR degradation.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing persistent PRLR (Figure 3F) and pS9-GSK3β (Figure 3E) in early lesions at involution.

claim: Precancerous cells in virgin mice do not activate PRLR and therefore cannot exploit ErbB2-mediated GSK3β inactivation for aberrant activation of PRLR-STAT5.
source: However, precancerous cells in virgin mice do not activate PRLR and therefore cannot exploit ErbB2-mediated GSK3β inactivation for aberrant activation of PRLR-STAT5.
evidence: This is inferred from the low PRLR and pSTAT5 levels in virgin early lesions despite presence of pS9-GSK3β.

claim: By 6 months post involution, as few pSTAT5+ cells (5.7 ± 2.2%) could be detected in early lesions of parous mice, as in virgin mice (p=0.3).
source: Of note, by 6 months post involution, as few pSTAT5+ cells (5.7 ± 2.2%) could be detected in early lesions of parous mice, as in virgin mice (p=0.3; n = 4 mice; data not shown), suggesting that with time, parity-induced elevated levels of pSTAT5 in parous mice subside.
evidence: This is based on quantification data (not shown in figures).

claim: The lesions that were positive for both caErbB2 and caSTAT5a were less apoptotic than the lesions induced in the contralateral glands by caErbB2 alone.
source: Importantly, the lesions that were positive for both caErbB2 and caSTAT5a were less apoptotic than the lesions induced in the contralateral glands by caErbB2 alone (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A with p=0.005.

claim: Proliferation rates in lesions positive for both caErbB2 and caSTAT5a and lesions with caErbB2 alone were similar.
source: Proliferation rates in these two sets of lesions were similar (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B with p=0.4.

claim: Mice infected only with RCAS-caStat5a did not form tumors.
source: As expected, the mice that were infected only with RCAS-caStat5a did not form tumors, while the co-infected mice developed tumors much more rapidly than the mice infected with RCAS-caErbb2 alone (p=0.0002; Figure 4A), consistent with previous reports of a pro-tumorigenic role for STAT5 in the breast (Furth et al., 2011).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Co-infected mice (RCAS-caErbb2 and RCAS-caStat5a) developed tumors much more rapidly than the mice infected with RCAS-caErbb2 alone (p=0.0002).
source: As expected, the mice that were infected only with RCAS-caStat5a did not form tumors, while the co-infected mice developed tumors much more rapidly than the mice infected with RCAS-caErbb2 alone (p=0.0002; Figure 4A), consistent with previous reports of a pro-tumorigenic role for STAT5 in the breast (Furth et al., 2011).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A with p=0.0002.

claim: The Kaplan–Meier tumor-free survival curve of the co-infected virgin mice became superimposable on that of the parous cohort of mice that was infected with RCAS-caErbb2 alone and subsequently impregnated.
source: Significantly, the Kaplan–Meier tumor-free survival curve of the co-infected virgin mice became superimposable on that of the parous cohort of mice from Figure 1A that was infected with RCAS-caErbb2 alone and subsequently impregnated (Figure 4A, red line).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Forced STAT5 activation in virgin mice is sufficient to mimic breast cancer promotion by pregnancy.
source: These results suggest that forced STAT5 activation in virgin mice is sufficient to mimic breast cancer promotion by pregnancy.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the tumor latency data in Figure 4A showing similar outcomes for co-infected virgin mice and parous mice.

claim: Among the experimental MMTV-tva virgin mice, a small subset (20%) exhibited high baseline levels of pSTAT5 in both the normal mammary epithelium and early lesions, while the rest had barely detectable pSTAT5 in either.
source: Among the experimental MMTV-tva virgin mice that were euthanized at 8.5 weeks post RCAS-caErbb2 infection (described in Figure 1C–E), a small subset (20%) exhibited high baseline levels of pSTAT5 in both the normal mammary epithelium and early lesions, while the rest had barely detectable pSTAT5 in either (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Apoptosis levels were inversely correlated with levels of pSTAT5 in early lesions from pSTAT5hi and pSTAT5lo groups of mice.
source: Apoptosis levels were inversely correlated with levels of pSTAT5 in early lesions from these two groups of mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B with p=0.03 and R²=0.5628.

claim: The pSTAT5hi sub-cohort exhibited a shorter tumor-free survival than the pSTAT5lo mice and became indistinct from that of the parous cohort.
source: Moreover, when we reanalyzed the data among the experimental virgin mice from Figure 1A, the pSTAT5hi sub-cohort exhibited a shorter tumor-free survival than the pSTAT5lo mice and, remarkably, became indistinct from that of the parous cohort from Figure 1A (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B with p=0.01.

claim: High baseline pSTAT5 levels in virgin mice mimic stimulation of breast carcinogenesis by pregnancy.
source: These observations suggest that high baseline pSTAT5 levels in virgin mice mimic stimulation of breast carcinogenesis by pregnancy.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the tumor latency data in Figure 4B showing similar outcomes for pSTAT5hi virgin mice and parous mice.

claim: The infected cells in WAP-tva mice harbored significantly more pSTAT5+ cells (threefold) than did the infected cells in MMTV-tva mice.
source: As predicted, the infected cells in this line harbored significantly more pSTAT5+ cells (threefold) than did the infected cells in MMTV-tva mice, while the pSTAT5+ proportion among the uninfected cells remained comparable between the two lines of mice (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C with p=0.007.

claim: There were many more pSTAT5+ cells in the resulting early lesions in WAP-tva mice than in MMTV-tva mice.
source: As predicted, there were many more pSTAT5+ cells in the resulting early lesions in WAP-tva mice than in MMTV-tva mice (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C with p=0.007.

claim: The apoptosis rate was lower in the early lesions in WAP-tva mice than in MMTV-tva mice.
source: The apoptosis rate was lower in the early lesions in WAP-tva mice (Figure 4D), while proliferation remained comparable (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D with p=0.004.

claim: Proliferation remained comparable between early lesions in WAP-tva and MMTV-tva mice.
source: The apoptosis rate was lower in the early lesions in WAP-tva mice (Figure 4D), while proliferation remained comparable (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3 with p=0.8.

claim: Mammary tumors arose more rapidly in WAP-tva mice than in MMTV-tva mice.
source: Mammary tumors also arose more rapidly (Figure 4E) and with greater multiplicity (Figure 4—figure supplement 4) in WAP-tva mice than in MMTV-tva mice, consistent with previous evidence of alveolar or alveolar progenitor cells as the preferred cell of origin for ErbB2-initiated mammary tumors (Li et al., 2003; Andrechek et al., 2004; Henry et al., 2004; Jeselsohn et al., 2010).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4E with p=0.02.

claim: Mammary tumors arose with greater multiplicity in WAP-tva mice than in MMTV-tva mice.
source: Mammary tumors also arose more rapidly (Figure 4E) and with greater multiplicity (Figure 4—figure supplement 4) in WAP-tva mice than in MMTV-tva mice, consistent with previous evidence of alveolar or alveolar progenitor cells as the preferred cell of origin for ErbB2-initiated mammary tumors (Li et al., 2003; Andrechek et al., 2004; Henry et al., 2004; Jeselsohn et al., 2010).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4 with p=0.0001.

claim: The STAT5-activated subset of mammary epithelial cells has a compromised apoptotic response to oncogenic insult and is highly vulnerable to oncogene-induced carcinogenesis even without a pregnancy.
source: These data demonstrate that the STAT5-activated subset of mammary epithelial cells has a compromised apoptotic response to oncogenic insult and is highly vulnerable to oncogene-induced carcinogenesis even without a pregnancy.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the data from WAP-tva mice showing reduced apoptosis and accelerated tumorigenesis (Figures 4C-E).

claim: In WAP-tva mice infected by RCAS-caErbb2, pregnancy could no longer accelerate the already hastened tumorigenesis.
source: More importantly, in WAP-tva mice infected by RCAS-caErbb2, pregnancy could no longer accelerate the already hastened tumorigenesis (Figure 4F), directly implicating STAT5 in mediating pregnancy's stimulation of breast carcinogenesis.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4F with p=0.9.

claim: STAT5 activation during pregnancy is sufficient to increase the survival of precancerous cells and to promote their progression to cancer.
source: Together, we conclude that STAT5 activation during pregnancy is sufficient to increase the survival of precancerous cells and to promote their progression to cancer.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the collective data from Figures 4A-F showing that STAT5 activation mimics pregnancy's effects on tumorigenesis.

claim: The Stat5a knockout mice on the FVB background showed normal mammary development during pregnancy, lactation, and involution.
source: The Stat5a knockout mice on the FVB background showed normal mammary development during pregnancy, lactation, and involution (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) unlike those on the 129 background (Liu et al., 1997).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The early lesions in Stat5a−/− parous mice exhibited significantly lower levels of pSTAT5 than did the lesions in Stat5a+/+ mice.
source: When these Stat5a−/− mice were bred to MMTV-tva mice, infected with RCAS-caErbb2, impregnated 4 days post infection, and analyzed at I10, the resultant early lesions exhibited significantly lower levels of pSTAT5 than did the lesions in Stat5a+/+ mice (Figure 5A) confirming the predominance of STAT5a in the mammary gland.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A with p=0.007.

claim: Early lesions in Stat5a−/− parous mice showed a level of apoptosis both comparable to that of early lesions in the age-matched virgin control mice and significantly higher than that of early lesions of Stat5a+/+ mice at I10.
source: These lesions showed a level of apoptosis both comparable to that of early lesions in the age-matched virgin control mice and significantly higher than that of early lesions of Stat5a+/+ mice at I10 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B with p=0.007.

claim: The number and size of early lesions were similar in parous vs virgin Stat5a−/− mice.
source: The number and size of early lesions were also similar in parous vs virgin Stat5a−/− mice (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C-D with p=0.63 and p=0.54.

claim: Tumor incidence and tumor latency were similar in parous vs virgin Stat5a−/− mice.
source: Importantly, tumor incidence and tumor latency were similar in parous vs virgin Stat5a−/− mice (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E-F with p=0.59 and p=0.89.

claim: Stat5a is necessary for pregnancy-mediated promotion of preneoplastic cell survival, lesion progression, and tumorigenesis.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that Stat5a is necessary for pregnancy-mediated promotion of preneoplastic cell survival, lesion progression, and tumorigenesis.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the data in Figure 5 showing that Stat5a deletion abolishes pregnancy's effects on early lesions and tumorigenesis.

claim: AG490 decreased pSTAT5, BclXL, and cell survival in parous early lesions, and induced lesion regression.
source: AG490 (75, or 200 mg/kg body weight) (Levitzki and Gazit, 1995) or diluent (DMSO) was administered every other day for 5 days starting from I2 to early lesion-bearing mice that had already completed lactation. AG490 decreased pSTAT5, BclXL, and cell survival in parous early lesions, and induced lesion regression (Figure 6A–C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A-C with p values of 0.02, 0.002, and 0.02.

claim: In virgin mice, AG490 did not have any significant impact on precancerous cell pSTAT5 positivity, apoptosis or early lesion regression.
source: In virgin mice, AG490 did not have any significant impact on precancerous cell pSTAT5 positivity, apoptosis or early lesion regression (Figure 6A–C), in accordance with the low levels of pSTAT5 in these lesions.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A-C with p values of 0.6, 0.6, and 0.81.

claim: AG490 did not affect pSTAT1, pSTAT3 or pSTAT6 positivity in either parous or virgin early lesions.
source: Of note, AG490 did not affect pSTAT1, pSTAT3 or pSTAT6 positivity in either parous or virgin early lesions (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In parous mice ruxolitinib decreased pSTAT5, blocked cell survival, and induced regression of early lesions.
source: Using a similar experimental approach, we found that in parous mice ruxolitinib also decreased pSTAT5, blocked cell survival, and induced regression of early lesions (Figure 6E–F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D-F with p values of 0.04, 0.02, and 0.02.

claim: Jak2 signaling is required for early lesion survival and progression.
source: Together, these findings suggest that Jak2 signaling is required for early lesion survival and progression and that blocking the upstream tyrosine kinase activity of STAT5 can prevent the progression of early lesions in parous mice.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the effects of AG490 and ruxolitinib shown in Figure 6A-F.

claim: Blocking the upstream tyrosine kinase activity of STAT5 can prevent the progression of early lesions in parous mice.
source: Together, these findings suggest that Jak2 signaling is required for early lesion survival and progression and that blocking the upstream tyrosine kinase activity of STAT5 can prevent the progression of early lesions in parous mice.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the effects of AG490 and ruxolitinib shown in Figure 6A-F.

claim: C188-9 caused a significant decrease in pSTAT5+ and BclXL+ cells in early lesions of parous mice.
source: C188-9 (100 mg/kg BW) or diluent (DMSO) was injected intraperitoneally into mice bearing RCAS-caErbb2-initiated early lesions only twice (I2 and I9). 1 day after the second injection (I10), C188-9 caused a significant decrease in pSTAT5+ and BclXL+ cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A) but did not significantly reduce the low frequency of cells positive for pSTAT1, pSTAT3, or pSTAT6 (p=0.2, 0.6, and 0.8, respectively; Figure 6—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A with p=0.005.

claim: C188-9 did not significantly reduce the low frequency of cells positive for pSTAT1, pSTAT3, or pSTAT6 in early lesions.
source: C188-9 (100 mg/kg BW) or diluent (DMSO) was injected intraperitoneally into mice bearing RCAS-caErbb2-initiated early lesions only twice (I2 and I9). 1 day after the second injection (I10), C188-9 caused a significant decrease in pSTAT5+ and BclXL+ cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A) but did not significantly reduce the low frequency of cells positive for pSTAT1, pSTAT3, or pSTAT6 (p=0.2, 0.6, and 0.8, respectively; Figure 6—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3B with p values of 0.2, 0.6, and 0.8.

claim: C188-9 caused a significant rise in apoptosis in the lesions of parous mice.
source: Further, C188-9 caused a significant rise in apoptosis in the lesions of parous mice, (Figure 6G) while having no detectable effect on proliferation (Figure 6—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6G with p=0.003.

claim: C188-9 had no detectable effect on proliferation in early lesions of parous mice.
source: Further, C188-9 caused a significant rise in apoptosis in the lesions of parous mice, (Figure 6G) while having no detectable effect on proliferation (Figure 6—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3C with p=0.6.

claim: C188-9 caused a dramatic regression of parous premalignant lesions.
source: Importantly, C188-9 caused a dramatic regression of parous premalignant lesions (Figure 6H, Figure 6—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6H with p=0.03.

claim: In virgin mice, even four doses of C188-9 did not result in a significant decrease of pSTAT5+ cells, increase of apoptosis, or decrease of size in early lesions.
source: This effect is unlikely to be caused by off-target impact: in virgin mice, even four doses of C188-9 did not result in a significant decrease of pSTAT5+ cells, increase of apoptosis, or decrease of size in early lesions (p=0.6, 0.8, and 0.7, respectively; n = 3 mice; data not shown).
evidence: This is based on quantification data (not shown in figures).

claim: Short-term treatment with C188-9 led to a significant reduction in tumor incidence in parous mice.
source: This short-term treatment led to a significant reduction in tumor incidence: by 3 months post ErbB2 activation, only three of the eight C188-9-treated mice had developed palpable tumors, while all 10 diluent-treated parous mice had done so (Figure 6J).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6J with p=0.001.

claim: Short-term treatment with C188-9 led to a significant improvement in tumor-free survival in the parous group.
source: This regimen also led to a significant improvement in tumor-free survival in the parous group (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6I with p=0.0006.

claim: The tumor-free survival curve of C188-9-treated parous mice became superimposable on that of the age-matched virgin group that was similarly treated.
source: In fact, the tumor-free survival curve became superimposable on that of the age-matched virgin group that was similarly treated.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6I.

claim: C188-9 did not significantly affect either tumor incidence or latency in virgin mice.
source: It is important to note that C188-9 did not significantly affect either tumor incidence or latency in virgin mice (p=0.6 and 0.5, respectively; Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4 with p values of 0.6 and 0.48.

claim: A short-term treatment with C188-9 hindered the progression of preexisting early lesions and removed the stimulatory effect of pregnancy on breast cancer risk.
source: Therefore, a short-term treatment with C188-9 hindered the progression of preexisting early lesions and removed the stimulatory effect of pregnancy on breast cancer risk.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the tumor incidence and latency data in Figure 6I-J.

claim: A short-term prophylactic treatment with inhibitors blocking Jak2-STAT5 signaling may lower breast cancer risk for women who have had a late-age first pregnancy and have already completed lactation.
source: Together, these preclinical data suggest that a short-term prophylactic treatment with inhibitors blocking Jak2-STAT5 signaling may lower breast cancer risk for women who have had a late-age first pregnancy and have already completed lactation.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the preclinical data in Figure 6.

claim: Significantly more pSTAT5+ lesions were detected in parous cases than in nulliparous cases of DCIS from women.
source: Indeed, when we compared 14 cases of DCIS (preinvasive lesions) from women who had a pregnancy 6–25 years prior to diagnosis with 13 cases from age-matched nulliparous women in a tissue bank from the University of Colorado (Figure 7—source data 1A), we detected significantly more pSTAT5+ lesions in the parous cases than in the nulliparous cases (p=0.01; Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A-B with p=0.01.

claim: Patients with higher percentages of pSTAT5+ cells within their lesions also had higher percentages of pSTAT5+ cells in the lesion-adjacent, histopathologically benign breast epithelium.
source: Interestingly, patients with higher percentages of pSTAT5+ cells within their lesions also had higher percentages of pSTAT5+ cells in the lesion-adjacent, histopathologically benign breast epithelium (which may be abnormal at genetic, epigenetic and gene expression levels) (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C-D with p<0.0001 and R²=0.6664.

claim: pSTAT5 levels in histopathologically 'normal' breast epithelia may predict breast cancer risk in women.
source: This observation suggests that pSTAT5 levels in histopathologically 'normal' breast epithelia may predict breast cancer risk in women.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between pSTAT5 in benign epithelia and DCIS shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Higher pSTAT5 in tumor-adjacent breast epithelia retrospectively predicted accelerated development of breast cancer following a full-term pregnancy (p=0.007).
source: Therefore, we also quantified pSTAT5+ cell frequencies in tumor-adjacent breast epithelia (≥5.0 cm away from an invasive cancer) from a cohort of 24 breast cancer patients diagnosed at the M.D. Anderson Cancer Center (Figure 7E). Higher pSTAT5 in these breast epithelia retrospectively predicted accelerated development of breast cancer following a full-term pregnancy (p=0.007; Figure 7F) with all other characteristics being comparable (Figure 7—source data 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7E-F with p=0.007.

claim: STAT5 is involved in pregnancy's promotion of long-term risk of sporadic human breast cancer.
source: Although the sample size of these two cohorts is relatively small, they nevertheless suggest an involvement of STAT5 in pregnancy's promotion of long-term risk of sporadic human breast.
evidence: This is inferred from the human cohort data in Figure 7.

claim: Normal mammary epithelial cells in fully involuted mammary glands—in the event of suffering an oncogenic mutation—do not aberrantly activate STAT5 signaling and can successfully initiate an apoptosis response to evade carcinogenesis.
source: Therefore, normal breast epithelial cells in the fully involuted mammary gland—in the event of suffering an oncogenic mutation—do not aberrantly activate STAT5 signaling and can successfully initiate an apoptosis response to evade carcinogenesis.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the data in Figure 8A-B showing low pSTAT5 and high apoptosis in lesions arising after involution.

claim: Mammary cells in involuted glands responded to caErbB2 with a lower proliferation rate than the cells in virgin mice.
source: Furthermore, we found that the mammary cells in these involuted glands responded to caErbB2 with a lower proliferation rate than the cells in virgin mice (Figure 8C–E), demonstrating that the slowly proliferating mammary cells of involuted mammary glands are also indolent to aberrant proliferation initiated by a future oncogenic mutation, as previously suggested (Guzman et al., 1999; Medina et al., 2001).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8C-E with p=0.03.

claim: The slowly proliferating mammary cells of involuted mammary glands are indolent to aberrant proliferation initiated by a future oncogenic mutation.
source: Furthermore, we found that the mammary cells in these involuted glands responded to caErbB2 with a lower proliferation rate than the cells in virgin mice (Figure 8C–E), demonstrating that the slowly proliferating mammary cells of involuted mammary glands are also indolent to aberrant proliferation initiated by a future oncogenic mutation, as previously suggested (Guzman et al., 1999; Medina et al., 2001).
evidence: This is inferred from the proliferation data in Figure 8C-E and supported by citations (Guzman et al., 1999; Medina et al., 2001).

claim: Pregnancy causes mammary cells that have not mutated to become resistant to transformation by a future oncogenic insult, but instigates whichever mammary cells have already mutated to progress to cancer.
source: These results, when combined with our data on pregnancy's instigation of preexisting precancerous cells, suggest the following overall hypothesis: pregnancy causes mammary cells that have not mutated to become resistant to transformation by a future oncogenic insult, but instigates whichever mammary cells have already mutated to progress to cancer.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the combined data in Figures 1-8.

claim: The age-dependent effect of pregnancy on breast cancer risk in women may be due to age-associated gradual accumulation of mutated cells and early lesions which are stimulated by a delayed pregnancy to progress to cancer.
source: Therefore, the age-dependent effect of pregnancy on breast cancer risk in women may be due to age-associated gradual accumulation of mutated cells and early lesions which are stimulated by a delayed pregnancy to progress to cancer.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the overall findings of the study.

claim: Brief prophylactic treatment with anti-Jak2/STAT5 inhibitors induced apoptosis in early lesions and caused them to regress, and led to significant delay in tumor appearance.
source: Envisioning an application in preventing breast cancer in women having a late age pregnancy who may have already accumulated precancerous cells, we prophylactically treated fully involuted, early lesion-bearing mice with several small molecule inhibitors targeting Jak2 or STAT5 activity. This brief treatment induced apoptosis in early lesions and caused them to regress, and importantly led to significant delay in tumor appearance.
evidence: This is based on the data in Figure 6 showing effects of AG490, ruxolitinib, and C188-9.

claim: Prophylactic therapy targeting Jak2-STAT5 signaling may lower breast cancer risk in high risk women.
source: pSTAT5 is detected in human breast early lesions, especially in women who have had a pregnancy; therefore, prophylactic therapy targeting Jak2-STAT5 signaling may lower breast cancer risk in high risk women.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the preclinical data in Figure 6 and human data in Figure 7.

claim: This alternative prevention modality may require only a short-term treatment after pregnancy and lactation; thus, it may be more acceptable to women who are as yet breast cancer-free.
source: The alternative prevention modality indicated by our results may require only a short-term treatment after pregnancy and lactation; thus, it may be more acceptable to women who are as yet breast cancer-free.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the short-term treatment regimen used in the mouse studies.

claim: This new chemoprevention strategy may prevent ER-positive cancer as well as other subtypes.
source: Additionally, unlike current prevention strategies (Bode and Dong, 2009), this alternative regimen may prevent ER-positive cancer as well as other subtypes: ER is negative in 71% of caErbB2-initiated tumors and in 63% of Wnt1-induced tumors in our parous mice although ER is present in the great majority of early lesions induced by either caErbB2 or Wnt1 (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on ER status data (not shown in figures) from tumors in the mouse models.

claim: Even in nulliparous mice or women, increased pSTAT5 in precancerous cells promotes tumorigenesis, and blocking STAT5 activity may also reduce their risk of breast cancer.
source: These observations suggest that even in nulliparous mice or women, increased pSTAT5 in precancerous cells promotes tumorigenesis, and blocking STAT5 activity may also reduce their risk of breast cancer.
evidence: This is inferred from the data in Figure 4 showing effects of baseline pSTAT5 levels in virgin mice.

claim: pSTAT5 in premalignant breast lesions in women may predict a higher chance of progression to clinical cancer.
source: Our data suggest that pSTAT5 in premalignant breast lesions in women may predict a higher chance of progression to clinical cancer, and therefore may help differentiate high risk vs low risk patients and may affect treatment and prevention options.
evidence: This is inferred from the human cohort data in Figure 7 and the mouse model data showing correlation between pSTAT5 and tumor progression.

claim: Increased pSTAT5 even in histopathologically normal breast epithelia may predict a high risk of breast cancer.
source: Moreover, increased pSTAT5 even in histopathologically normal breast epithelia may predict a high risk of breast cancer: as discussed in the preceding paragraph, increased baseline levels of pSTAT5 in normal mammary epithelia in nulliparous mice were correlated with higher pSTAT5 levels and lower apoptosis in early lesions of nulliparous mice and predicted an accelerated evolution to overt cancer; pSTAT5 levels were also higher in histologically normal mammary epithelium in MMTV-Erbb2 mice; and importantly, pSTAT5 was elevated in histologically normal breast epithelia adjacent to DCIS with increased pSTAT5, and high pSTAT5 in tumor-adjacent normal appearing breast epithelia predicted shorter time from the last pregnancy to cancer diagnosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data in Figures 4 and 7 showing correlations between pSTAT5 in normal epithelia and cancer risk.

claim: pSTAT5 levels in normal breast epithelia may serve as a biomarker for estimating the efficacy of anti-Jak2/STAT5 and other chemopreventive strategies.
source: It is also possible that pSTAT5 levels in normal breast epithelia may serve as a biomarker for estimating the efficacy of anti-Jak2/STAT5 and other chemopreventive strategies.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed correlations between pSTAT5 levels and cancer risk.
